strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem: validating neural posterior estimation (NPE) models, which is crucial for reliability and safety in simulation-based inference (SBI).

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) provides a solid mathematical justification for why the conformal C2ST maintains power even when the underlying classifier is weak or poorly trained, showing that the expected p-value degrades gently with the L2 estimation error.

The experimental design is exceptionally strong, particularly the 'stress test' where classifiers are systematically degraded by interpolating weights with a randomly initialized model. This directly and elegantly validates the paper's core premise.
The paper is clearly written, logically organized, and begins with a helpful toy example that builds immediate intuition.
weaknesses: The core idea of using conformal calibration for two-sample testing is heavily built on the framework of Hu & Lei (2024), which somewhat limits the algorithmic novelty, although the specialization to SBI and the theoretical analysis of weak classifiers are distinct contributions.

High simulation complexity: The 'uniform test' requires $m$ calibration samples from the true joint distribution $p(\theta, y)$ for each of the $n_q$ test points, leading to a total of $n_q \times m$ simulations. Since SBI is designed for scenarios where simulations are computationally expensive, this sample complexity represents a significant bottleneck that limits the practical applicability of the highest-performing variant of the proposed method.

strengths: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, clearly structured, and easy to follow. The motivation for why standard C2ST fails (requiring a strong classifier) is well addressed.

The paper provides a solid theoretical foundation. Building on Hu & Lei (2024), the authors provide a nice theoretical result (Theorem 1) bounding the expected p-value's deviation under estimation error of the density ratio. This directly supports the claim that 'weak classifiers' are still highly effective.

The empirical evaluation is thorough, covering multiple failure modes of NPE (mean shift, covariance scaling, anisotropic perturbation, heavy-tailed, mode collapse, additional mode) and comparing against strong baselines (C2ST, SBC, TARP) as well as evaluating on high-dimensional manifold settings.

The illustrative toy examples (shift and rotation of classifier boundary) provide excellent, intuitive clarity on why the conformal method maintains power when the classifier's decision boundary is degraded.
weaknesses: The proposed 'Conformal Uniform' test requires generating a fresh calibration set of size $m$ for each of the $n_q$ test points. While drawing samples from the true joint $p(\theta, y)$ is typically cheap in simulation-based inference, this still requires $m \times n_q$ passes through the classifier. For $m=200$ and $n_q=1000$, this is 200,000 classifier evaluations, compared to only $n_p + n_q$ for standard C2ST or Conformal Multiple. The manuscript would benefit from a more explicit discussion or a table detailing the computational runtime trade-off.

The paper builds heavily on Hu & Lei (2024), and the primary algorithmic distinction is the transition from a shared calibration set (Conformal Multiple) to independent calibration sets (Conformal Uniform). While Conformal Uniform is shown to have better statistical power, the conceptual novelty relative to Hu & Lei (2024) is somewhat incremental, though the application to NPE and the specific robustness bounds under estimation error are valuable.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and challenging problem in Simulation-Based Inference (SBI): validating multidimensional neural posterior estimates (NPE).
Provides exact, finite-sample Type-I error control under the null hypothesis, which is a major improvement over classical C2ST that only controls Type-I error asymptotically.

Provides a robust theoretical analysis, including Theorem 1, which bounds the deviation of the expected p-value under an estimated density ratio from the oracle density ratio, demonstrating robustness to weak classifiers.

The empirical evaluation is thorough, benchmarking against standard baselines (SBC, TARP, C2ST) on several controlled posterior perturbations and demonstrating superior power and robustness to classifier degradation.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as the paper heavily builds on the conformal two-sample testing framework introduced by Hu & Lei (2024) [1].

The 'uniform test' variant requires a fresh calibration set for each test point. In high-dimensional regimes with many test points, generating $n_q \times m$ samples and passing them through the classifier introduces significant computational overhead.

In many practical SBI applications, running the simulator to obtain $y \sim p(y | \theta)$ is the primary bottleneck. If the simulator is computationally expensive, generating a large calibration set from the true joint $p(\theta, y)$ is impractical, which limits the real-world utility of the high-power 'uniform test' variant.
Minor editorial and formatting errors, such as 'modeling have have made' in Section 1, 'Covraiance Scaling' in the caption of Figure 6, and hard-to-read legends in Figure 1.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation, proving both finite-sample Type-I error control for the uniform test and a graceful $O(\epsilon^{2/3})$ degradation of power as the classifier's quality degrades.
A very practical contribution that directly addresses a major bottleneck of standard Classifier Two-Sample Tests (C2ST)—the reliance on highly accurate or Bayes-optimal classifiers.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation covering synthetic posterior perturbations, high-dimensional image corruptions on CIFAR-10, and a realistic scientific simulation task (gravitational lensing), demonstrating superior power and robustness over multiple state-of-the-art baselines.
Excellent writing, clear structure, and highly useful qualitative additions such as the 'Practitioner's Guide' which translates theoretical trade-offs into actionable advice.
weaknesses: The core conformal testing framework is heavily based on Hu & Lei (2024); while the orthogonal focus on robustness theory and the equal-marginal conditional setup is highly valuable, the purely algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental.

The uniform test requires generating fresh calibration samples from the reference distribution for each test point, which can be computationally prohibitive when the reference simulator is expensive (though this is partially mitigated by the proposed Multiple test variant).

The uniform test relies on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test to evaluate uniformity, but other tests (like Anderson-Darling) are often more sensitive to tail deviations of p-values; a brief discussion or comparison of these alternative statistical tests is missing.

strengths: Strong Theoretical Guarantees: The paper provides rigorous proof of both finite-sample Type-I error control (for the Uniform variant) and asymptotic validity (for the Multiple variant). More importantly, it establishes a robustness theory (Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 4.2) showing that the test power degrades gracefully as O(epsilon^{2/3}) with classifier estimation error, which mathematically justifies why weak classifiers can still perform well.

Thorough Empirical Evaluation: The method is evaluated on a diverse set of tasks: controlled Gaussian/NPE perturbations, high-dimensional image corruptions (CIFAR-10), and a realistic, high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (gravitational lensing). It consistently outperforms standard C2ST and other specialized baselines (SBC, TARP, DC, MMDFuse).

High Presentation Quality: The paper is exceptionally clear and well-structured. The toy example in Section 1 and the 'Practitioner's Guide' in Appendix D make the paper highly accessible and useful for practitioners.

Practical Significance: Standard C2ST's reliance on near-optimal classifiers is a known bottleneck. By showing that a simple rank-based conformal calibration can bypass this requirement, this paper provides a highly practical diagnostic tool for generative modeling and neural posterior estimation.
weaknesses: Incremental Algorithmic Novelty: The core conformal testing framework is largely inherited from Hu & Lei (2024). While the application to C2ST/NPE and the robustness theory under weak classifiers are novel, the algorithmic formulation itself (equation 1) is not a major departure from existing literature.

Computational and Sample Overhead of the Uniform Test: The exact finite-sample validity (Lemma 3.1) is only guaranteed for the Conformal Uniform test, which requires drawing m fresh calibration samples from p for every test point from q (resulting in m * N samples from p). While this is feasible in NPE where the simulator is cheap, it restricts the applicability of the exact test in cases where sampling from p is expensive.

Asymptotic Nature of the Budget-Matched Test: The Conformal Multiple test, which matches the budget of standard C2ST, only enjoys asymptotic validity (Theorem A.8) rather than exact finite-sample guarantees.

strengths: Strong Practical Motivation: Successfully tackles the open challenge of utilizing weak or imperfectly trained classifiers for reliable two-sample testing. This is highly relevant for validating modern deep generative models and Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) where finding the Bayes-optimal decision boundary is difficult.

Rigorous Theoretical Analysis: Establishes solid theoretical guarantees for robustness under estimation errors. Theorems 3.5 and 4.2 show that the testing power degrades gracefully (at a rate of O(ε^{2/3})) as the classifier deviates from the Bayes-optimal, under mild assumptions.

Thorough and Realistic Evaluation: The experimental setup is excellent, demonstrating performance across synthetic posterior perturbations, high-dimensional image corruptions (CIFAR-10), and a practical astrophysics simulation (gravitational lensing). The classifier degradation experiments (using parameter interpolation) provide a clear 'stress test' that validates the robustness claim.
Excellent Presentation: The paper is highly readable, structured logically, and includes a helpful 'Practitioner's Guide' that translates theoretical insights into concrete recommendations.
weaknesses: Incremental Algorithmic Novelty: The paper's conformal framework and the U-statistic formulation for the multiple test are heavily inherited from Hu & Lei (2024). While the motivation (robustness to weak classifiers) and the specific application to joint/conditional distributions with equal marginals are distinct, the algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited.

Sample Complexity of the Uniform Test: The exact finite-sample Type-I error control of the Conformal Uniform test relies on drawing fresh calibration sets for each test point. This requires m * N samples from p, which can become a bottleneck when the simulator p is computationally expensive (even though the multiple test avoids this, it only offers asymptotic validity).

Incomplete Baseline Comparisons in Image Experiments: In Figure 3 (CIFAR-10 experiments), only C2ST and its conformal variants are evaluated. Including other general-purpose two-sample tests (like MMDFuse) in these high-dimensional image experiments would strengthen the empirical claims.
